authors.name: Rowan Vale
authors.bio: The man behind The Pecking Order. Rowan trades in sharp verdicts, spectacular reversals and an unwavering belief that this week finally explained everything. His inbox rarely agrees.

authors.name: Mara Voss
authors.bio: Mara follows the details that outlast the scoreboard: protection, personnel, responsibility and the choices that turn a talented roster into a contender.

authors.name: Ellis Quill
authors.bio: Ellis writes The Long Season, a column about the people and expectations beneath the standings. A bad afternoon is evidence, not a complete biography.

authors.name: Dorian Pike
authors.bio: Dorian asks the awkward question, counts the points and keeps asking. The Uncomfortable Truth takes the league’s overlooked clubs seriously.

authors.name: Tessa Wren
authors.bio: Tessa studies the matchups, names the pressure points and puts a score beside every pick. She covers the entire weekly slate for The Week Ahead.

authors.name: Calvin Rook
authors.bio: Calvin covers the college game and the next IFL class. The Rook Board is built around projection, athletic traits and the occasional prospect he refuses to stop believing in.

articles.title: Forty-four unanswered. Four weeks without Brooks.
articles.dek: Archam Manning turned the second-half kickoff into an 86-yard touchdown, Gengar Pickens caught two more, and Saffron overwhelmed Pastoria. The injury report made the celebration complicated.
articles.author: rowan-vale

body.text: Saffron spent the first half giving Pastoria reasons to believe. Then Archam Manning took the opening kickoff of the second half and returned it 86 yards for a touchdown. The quarterback had apparently decided that waiting for the offense to take the field was an unnecessary administrative step. The Psi Corps won 44–9, scored the final 44 points and improved to 6–1. A game they trailed at halftime finished as their loudest possible argument for attention.

The next argument will concern the defense. Verrick Brooks, the league's sacks leader with thirteen, is listed out four weeks after this game. Ninetales also has a four-week absence. Trent Scarboro leaves with a magnificent second-half score and two substantial holes to address before Sootopolis visits. The scoreboard is an invitation to celebrate. The personnel list will be waiting when the celebration ends.

Manning completed 23 of 36 passes for 350 yards, three touchdowns and an interception. He also supplied the return that turned a 9–7 deficit into a lead Saffron never surrendered. Gengar Pickens caught seven passes for 176 yards and two scores, including a 48-yard gain that helped rescue the first half. Dam Skattebo added 82 rushing yards, a rushing touchdown and a 26-yard scoring reception. There were several routes out of the early trouble, and eventually the Psi Corps used most of them.
The return helped everybody breathe. We still had work after it. You don't get to keep the lead just because the first play after halftime went well.
body.speaker: Archam Manning

body.text: Pastoria had earned its lead

This was no ceremonial nine-point head start. Saffron's first two possessions traveled 46 and 58 yards and ended on downs. The second consumed fifteen plays and 3:19. Moving the ball looked achievable; finishing was another matter. Pastoria absorbed those possessions, collected Horsea's 53-yard field goal and then found the biggest offensive play of its afternoon.

With 2:24 remaining in the second quarter, Farigiraf threw deep middle to Kilowattrel for a 53-yard touchdown. The Waves led 9–0 after the missed extra point. Their scoring drive had covered 81 yards in four plays, including a twenty-yard completion to Seviper on third-and-one. Saffron had spent much more effort traveling less efficiently. For a while, the upset had a perfectly respectable football explanation.

Pickens changed the conversation. Manning found him deep right for 48 yards at the two-minute mark, then deep left for a ten-yard touchdown at 1:17. The four-play, 71-yard possession gave Saffron seven points and a useful demonstration of what its receivers could do once the throws started connecting. Pickens would finish with an average above twenty-five yards per reception. Pastoria could contest him; it could not afford to keep losing the contests at that distance.

The remaining seconds still contained a warning. After Dipplin and Granbull helped force a punt, Manning led another advancing possession but threw an interception to Dubwool with seventeen seconds left. Pastoria went to halftime ahead 9–7. Saffron had recovered its balance without yet taking control, a distinction that the final margin makes easy to forget.
We left too much out there early. I'm pleased with the catches. I'm not going to pretend those empty drives were acceptable because we won big afterward.
body.speaker: Gengar Pickens

body.text: The quarterback delivered the return himself

Horsea opened the third quarter with a squib kick. Manning returned it 86 yards for the touchdown, then threw the successful two-point pass to HeeDee Lamb. Saffron led 15–9 before running an ordinary offensive snap in the half. A quarterback who had just thrown a costly interception had supplied the fastest available reply.

Pastoria's next possession gained two yards and ended in a punt. Saffron followed with an eleven-play, 82-yard drive. The possession survived two sacks before Furfrou ran up the middle for an eight-yard touchdown on third-and-eight with 2:10 left in the quarter. Manning connected with Ariados for another two-point conversion. The Psi Corps had turned the halftime deficit into a 23–9 lead through a return, a sustained drive and two successful conversion throws.

Those two touchdowns had different engines. The return needed one enormous play. The next possession needed repeated answers, including a third-down run after the defense had pushed Manning backward. Together they explain why this became more than a collection of deep passes. Saffron converted seven of ten third downs and finished with eighteen first downs. Pastoria managed seven first downs and converted two of ten third downs.

The fourth quarter made the margin look merciless. Medicham intercepted Farigiraf at 5:41. Manning then threw short right to Skattebo for a 26-yard touchdown at 4:58. After another Pastoria punt, Pickens caught a deep-left pass for a 28-yard score at 3:13. Skattebo finished the scoring with a three-yard run up the middle with thirty-nine seconds left. Saffron scored 37 points after halftime and allowed none.
The defense's next assignment changed

Dipplin finished with two sacks and twelve pressures; Granbull added a sack and four pressures. Farigiraf was sacked three times in all. The Waves produced 217 total yards, including just 24 on sixteen rushing attempts. Kilowattrel's two catches accounted for 88 receiving yards, while Seviper caught six passes for 55. The early explosive completion was real. The sustained second-half threat never arrived.

That defensive performance now has to travel without Brooks and Ninetales. Brooks recorded two tackles and two tackles for loss in this game before appearing on the injury list. The records do not make every subsequent stop his replacement's achievement, and they do not tell us the precise moment the rotation changed. What is clear is that Scarboro will have to replace an important source of pressure for the next stretch. Thirteen sacks are a substantial job description.
We can enjoy what the whole group did and still be honest about the players we'll miss. The preparation changes. The responsibility to finish the next game doesn't.
body.speaker: Trent Scarboro

body.text: Pastoria falls to 2–5 and visits Violet next. Saffron hosts Sootopolis before a Week 10 trip to unbeaten Mossdeep. Those dates give the injury news immediate weight, although skipping directly to the Eclipse would ignore a defense that has work to do now. Manning's return and Pickens' two scores belong in the highlights. The four-week entries belong in the next meeting.

For the record book, the last Pastoria points arrived with 2:24 left in the second quarter. For the next opponent, the most alarming Saffron points arrived at the opening kickoff of the third. Manning traveled 86 yards, then stayed on the field to throw for two more.

art.alt: Gengar Pickens, Gengar No. 15, with a football in Saffron pink and sky blue.

articles.title: Lavender led by eleven. Hatterene missed twice all day.
articles.dek: A 66-yard Ninjask touchdown finished Blackthorn’s surge, as the Dragons turned a 17–6 deficit into a 27–17 win and handed the Wails another difficult finish.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: For more than half the afternoon, Lavender had a convincing answer to the previous week's embarrassment. The Wails opened with two touchdown drives, led Blackthorn 14–6 at halftime and extended the advantage to eleven points in the third quarter. Mr. Clanky was finding useful completions. Hobbes was finding room. A team beaten 63–10 by Mossdeep had given itself a very different game to discuss.

Then the discussion changed in twenty-four seconds of fourth-quarter clock. Hatterene threw a six-yard touchdown to Frosmoth at 3:22, giving Blackthorn its first lead. After a quick Lavender punt, the next Dragons snap became a short-right completion to Ninjask for a 66-yard touchdown at 2:58. Blackthorn had trailed by eleven earlier in the third quarter; now it led by ten. Blackthorn won 27–17 and improved to 6–1; Lavender fell to 4–3.

The Wails had made the opponent work for much of what it gained. They could not make Hatterene miss often enough. The Blackthorn quarterback completed 27 of 29 passes for 307 yards and three touchdowns without an interception. There are defeats in which a defense can identify a handful of damaging completions. This one also asks Lavender to account for the ordinary throws that kept those larger moments possible.
I suppose two incompletions leaves something for the meeting. I'd rather they spend a little time on the other twenty-seven, if the schedule allows.
body.speaker: Hatterene

body.text: Lavender's early work deserved better

The opening possession covered 75 yards in eleven plays. Mr. Clanky finished it with a three-yard short-left touchdown pass to Kricketune at 3:02 of the first quarter. After Cacturne's 54-yard field goal, the Wails traveled another 75 yards in eight plays. This time the finish was a deep-left throw to Kujira for nineteen yards with 4:22 remaining in the second. Lavender led 14–3 and had demonstrated two sustained ways to get across the field.

Hobbes supplied 89 yards on ten carries, an 8.9-yard average that gave Travis Scarboro's offense real help. Mr. Clanky added 22 rushing yards and completed fifteen of 22 passes for 168 yards, two touchdowns and an interception. Beedrill caught four passes for 57 yards; People Eater caught all three targets for 27. The passing line lacked Blackthorn's volume, but the Wails were not surviving solely on opponent errors.

Cacturne's second field goal, from 36 yards with eighteen seconds left in the half, cut the gap to 14–6. The Wails then forced a punt on Blackthorn's first possession after the break. They used the next possession to add Just a cactus' 42-yard field goal at 3:25 of the third quarter. The lead was 17–6. The defense had just returned the ball, and the offense had added points. There was a plausible route home from there.
We had the lead. We had chances after we lost it. Both parts belong to us.
body.speaker: Mr. Clanky

body.text: A completion, then another

Hatterene's response needed five plays and 76 yards. Seadra caught the decisive deep-right pass for a forty-yard touchdown at 2:00 of the third quarter. The extra point brought Blackthorn within four. The Dragons had spent the first half accepting field goals; now a single throw had made the margin feel much less accommodating.

Lavender's next possession moved only five yards. Beedrill sacked Mr. Clanky for three, and Leavanny added a five-yard sack on third-and-thirteen. That stop sent Blackthorn into the possession that would take the lead. Leavanny had also recorded a seven-yard sack earlier in the quarter. The pressure mattered at the point when Lavender needed to resume building the kind of drives that opened the game.

The Dragons did not hurry the next answer. Their ten-play, 71-yard possession lasted 3:02. At the start of the fourth quarter, Furret ran right for seven and then five. Hatterene followed with short completions to Exploud, Grovyle, Exploud, Grovyle and Seadra. Furret added eight yards left before the touchdown throw to Frosmoth. The sequence kept putting the defense back to work without allowing an incompletion to interrupt it.

Exploud caught all eight targets for 53 yards. Grovyle caught all seven for 67. Those fifteen catches were the less spectacular part of Hatterene's remarkable percentage, and perhaps the most exhausting. Ninjask's long score would become the defining image. Exploud and Grovyle supplied a steady set of answers before it.

The first two drives showed what we came here to do. We have to carry that standard past halftime. Once they started stacking completions, we needed a stop and another possession with some length to it.
body.speaker: Travis Scarboro

body.text: Twenty-four seconds that changed the finish

After Frosmoth's touchdown and the extra point, Lavender took over at 3:19. Beedrill broke up a pass intended for Kujira. Mr. Clanky then completed a six-yard throw to Lavender's Beedrill, out of bounds, before another incompletion toward Kujira brought fourth down. Just a cactus punted, and Tinkaton's eighteen-yard return set Blackthorn up at its own 34.

The next play was the 66-yard touchdown. Hatterene threw short right to Ninjask, who finished the journey. A long gain does not have to begin with a long throw, a detail Lavender will have no difficulty remembering. Ninjask finished with three catches for 94 yards. Seadra had four for 59. Both receivers supplied touchdowns that changed the score more rapidly than the Wails could recover.

Lavender's final possession did offer another response. Completions to Frosmoth, People Eater and Carnivine, followed by runs from Diggersby and Mr. Clanky, moved the ball 48 yards. At the two-minute mark, however, Beedrill intercepted a deep-right throw and returned it twelve yards. Blackthorn ran twice, converted third-and-three with a five-yard pass to Grovyle and knelt twice. The Wails did not get another attempt.

Blackthorn gained 349 yards to Lavender's 294, while Lavender held a sixteen-to-thirteen advantage in first downs. Both teams converted two of six third downs. The totals describe a competitive afternoon; the final three Blackthorn touchdown possessions describe why it ended with daylight between them.

Lavender now hosts Sunyshore, another opponent arriving with six wins. Blackthorn hosts Veilstone. Scarboro can keep the evidence from those opening touchdown drives without treating it as compensation for the ending. The Wails led 17–6. Their next points never came. Hatterene's remaining completions were not required to be spectacular; enough of them simply kept the Dragons moving until Ninjask made one enormous.

art.alt: Hatterene No. 12 with a football in Blackthorn blue and cyan.

articles.title: Mt. Silver brings every department to 8–0
articles.dek: Jacoby Brizzet threw three touchdowns, Scep Smith Jr. returned a kickoff 95 yards, and Ninjask added a pick-six in the Reds’ 34–9 win over Snowpoint.
articles.author: dorian-pike

body.text: Mt. Silver can win while its quarterback completes fewer than half his passes. That is the uncomfortable news for everyone waiting for the Reds' injuries to catch up with them. Jacoby Brizzet finished eleven of 24 with two interceptions against Snowpoint. He also threw three touchdowns. The defense and return game added two more scores, and the Reds reached their bye at 8–0 with a 34–9 victory.

Connor McLarren's team has lost Josh Alakazam for an extended stretch and is still waiting on Garshawn Lynch. The replacements do not have to impersonate them on every snap when the rest of the team keeps supplying its own advantages. Scep Smith Jr. opened the second half with a 95-yard kickoff return for a touchdown. Ninjask intercepted Drampa and returned it 28 yards for another score in the fourth quarter. Five sacks helped keep Snowpoint's three scoring possessions limited to field goals.

That does not make Brizzet a passenger. His touchdown throws traveled 26 yards to Tony Gyarzalez, 41 to Gregar Jenings and four to Plusico Buress. The last came on fourth-and-four. There is a difference between an uneven performance and an irrelevant one. Brizzet's eleven completions produced 237 yards. Enough of them arrived with a large consequence attached.
If they're counting incompletions, I'm counting touchdowns. The coaches are welcome to count both. I have a feeling they'll insist.
body.speaker: Jacoby Brizzet

body.text: A long field did not slow the first answer

The Reds' opening scoring drive covered 96 yards in five plays. With 2:20 remaining in the first quarter, Brizzet threw short right to Gyarzalez for a 26-yard touchdown. The missed extra point left Mt. Silver ahead 6–0. Snowpoint had made the opponent begin far from the end zone. The Reds made the distance disappear remarkably quickly.

Gyarzalez finished with five catches for 91 yards, including a separate 29-yard gain. Jenings caught three passes for 109, with a longest gain of 62. Those two accounted for two hundred receiving yards between them. Snowpoint could force incompletions and still be punished severely when a pass did connect. Brizzet's completion percentage tells one part of the story; the distance traveled on the successful throws tells another.

The Blizzard responded with a 64-yard drive and Charjabug's thirty-yard field goal at the start of the second quarter. Medicham then intercepted Brizzet's short-right throw on the next Reds snap. Snowpoint had a chance to turn a mistake into a lead. Blayz Matthews sacked Drampa on third-and-eight, and Charjabug's 31-yard field goal tied the score at six instead.

That exchange matters more than the final margin suggests. The Reds had committed an immediate turnover after conceding points. Their defense kept the damage to three. Snowpoint had pulled even, but the opening was still narrow enough for Mt. Silver to close it with one productive possession. A defense that can reduce the price of a mistake gives an imperfect offense room to continue attacking.
There were difficult stretches. We kept getting another chance in a game that was still ours to influence. That makes it easier to settle down and do the next job.
body.speaker: Tony Gyarzalez

body.text: The pass rush kept the Blizzard cold

Matthews recorded another sack during the second quarter, this time for seven yards. Brizzet then found Jenings deep left for a 41-yard touchdown at 2:15. A two-play, 57-yard drive put the Reds ahead 13–6 after Adam Venutieri's extra point. Snowpoint had spent time assembling a tie; Mt. Silver needed less than half a minute of possession to take it away.

Scizor sacked Drampa twice before halftime, both for seven yards. Cranidos added a five-yard sack in the third quarter. Matthews and Scizor finished with two sacks each, Cranidos with one. Drampa completed fifteen of 28 passes for 141 yards, no touchdowns and an interception. The Blizzard punted seven times and converted only two of twelve third downs.

Snowpoint did find some rushing room. Oinkologne carried fifteen times for 78 yards, and the team finished with 99 on 23 attempts. Drakloak caught all four targets for 82 yards. Those gains prevented the offense from becoming entirely static. They did not produce a touchdown. Every time the Blizzard reached the scoreboard, Charjabug supplied the points with a kick.

McLarren's defense did not need to erase every yard to control the result. It needed to end the dangerous possessions without seven points. When the pass rush arrived, the distances became less forgiving. When Snowpoint managed to recover from an unfavorable down, the Reds still had enough margin to make the next stop count. The final thirteen-to-eleven first-down advantage belonged to Snowpoint. The touchdowns belonged to Mt. Silver.
The first play after halftime widened everything

Scep Smith Jr.'s 95-yard return at the beginning of the third quarter made it 20–6 after the extra point. The Reds did not need an offensive snap to extend the lead. Snowpoint then punted, and the Reds went seventy yards in eight plays. Brizzet took a sack near the end zone, but on fourth-and-four he threw short right to Buress for the touchdown. Mt. Silver led 27–6.

That fourth down was a significant answer. A sack and a difficult distance could have converted another promising drive into frustration. Buress caught his only target of the game, and it was the one that finished the possession. He did not need a large receiving total to make an essential contribution to the margin.

Brizzet's second interception, by Heatmor late in the third quarter, gave Snowpoint another opportunity. The Blizzard advanced 21 yards over nine plays and settled for Charjabug's 44-yard field goal with 5:32 left. At 27–9, the game still required a finish. Ninjask provided it at 3:06, intercepting a deep-right pass and returning it 28 yards for a touchdown. Venutieri added the final point.

Raticate then supplied the quiet ending. His last three carries gained nine, fifteen and twelve yards. He finished with 55 on nine attempts. A team capable of scoring on a kickoff and an interception could still end the game by handing the ball off and refusing to return it. Snowpoint's last possession had already ended in another punt.

Both clubs now have a bye. Snowpoint enters it at 2–6. Mt. Silver enters it with 205 points scored, 68 allowed and no losses. McLarren has time to examine the two interceptions without explaining away the result. The Reds scored through the air, on a return and on defense. The number beside their name is eight, and nobody has added the other number yet.

articles.title: Scol runs for 165. Sunyshore finally keeps the last possession.
articles.dek: The Starseekers beat Mahogany 17–10 behind 221 rushing yards and a second-half shutout, but Myles Gabite’s five-week injury changes the backfield ahead of Lavender.
articles.author: tessa-wren

body.text: Sunyshore had spent the previous week failing to finish its opportunities. Against Mahogany, the Starseekers eventually found the most dependable finish available: keep the ball until the clock runs out. Their last possession covered forty yards, included a third-down run from DeZhaun Watzon and ended with two kneels. A 17–10 victory moved Karson Jones' team to 6–2 and supplied a much better closing sequence than the one it left in Cerulean.

Scol Alexander made that ending possible long before the final drive. He ran eighteen times for 165 yards and a touchdown, averaging 9.2 yards per carry. Sunyshore totaled 221 rushing yards on 31 attempts. Mahogany managed 22 on twenty attempts. The passing games produced a much less flattering comparison for the home team, but the ground game and defense were strong enough to carry it.

The backfield will now change. Myles Gabite, who had four carries for 23 yards, is listed out five weeks. Fred Whirler is listed out one. The Starseekers cannot treat Alexander's production as proof that every future carry will be equally simple. They have a road game at Lavender next and a real absence to plan around, even after a performance that made their running game the clearest advantage on the field.
Some of the gains came early in a series, some kept a series alive. I'd want to separate those before saying we solved anything. The useful part is that we kept finding a run we could complete.
body.speaker: Scol Alexander

body.text: An eighty-yard opening statement

Sunyshore's first drive covered eighty yards in twelve plays and lasted 3:38. Alexander finished it with a four-yard run left at 2:22 of the first quarter. Duosion's extra point put the Starseekers ahead 7–0. It was a long, purposeful possession, the sort that allowed Jones' offense to establish the afternoon's most reliable source of progress.

The second drive also moved quickly, gaining 41 yards in three plays, but ended when Gabite fumbled after a five-yard run left. Bruxish recovered for Mahogany. The Frost used eleven plays to move 49 yards before settling for Watchog's 29-yard field goal. Conkel Jones' seven-yard sack on third-and-five helped keep the recovery from becoming seven points.

Sunyshore punted on its next possession, then immediately received the ball back through Ampharos' interception of a deep-left pass. Watzon finished the ensuing 38-yard drive with a three-yard short-middle touchdown pass to Sceptile. The Starseekers led 14–3 with 1:57 left before halftime. Their defense had created a shorter field, and the offense had converted it without demanding another long march.

Mahogany answered. Porygon-Z led an eight-play, 82-yard drive and threw short right to Wobbuffet for a three-yard touchdown with nineteen seconds remaining. The extra point cut the lead to 14–10. Golduck would finish with three catches for 94 yards, including a 42-yard gain. The Frost had enough passing production to keep Sunyshore from assuming its rushing advantage would settle the score by itself.

Watzon's final passing line was ten of eighteen for 97 yards, a touchdown and two interceptions. Fera LaGatr caught five passes for 62 yards; FLOAT SZN added two for nineteen. The Starseekers were productive when they ran and inconsistent when they threw, which made their next two possessions particularly uncomfortable.
Two interceptions, two defensive answers

After Mahogany opened the second half with a punt, Sunyshore advanced through runs of twelve, five and seven yards. Watzon then threw consecutive deep-right passes, the second intercepted by Frosmoth. The Frost had a chance to take the lead. They gained nine yards, failed on third down and punted.

Sunyshore's next possession began with a 23-yard completion to LaGatr, followed by runs of six and six. Watzon's deep-left throw was intercepted by Lopunny and returned 31 yards. Again Mahogany had the ball with the score 14–10. Again the defense prevented the mistake from becoming points. After a thirteen-yard completion to Sandy Shocks, Don Philliams stopped Exploud for a two-yard loss. An incompletion and a two-yard run left another punt.

Those two stops explain why Sunyshore's three turnovers did not become a losing afternoon. The Frost had opportunities. The Starseekers kept limiting their rushing gains and making the final down difficult. Mahogany finished with six first downs, converted two of nine third downs and punted five times. Every Frost possession in the second half ended with a punt.
I handed the defense two extra chores after halftime. They finished both, which is generous of them. I'd prefer to bring something more useful to the next meeting.
body.speaker: DeZhaun Watzon

body.text: Jones can accept the joke without accepting the interceptions. The two drives had already found productive runs before the throws went wrong. That is a concrete preparation issue for Lavender: preserve the gains that are available and make the next decision worthy of them. The defense bought time to work through it this week. The next opponent may attach a higher price.
Third-and-ten belonged to Alexander

The drive that produced the final points began with Alexander runs of ten and thirteen yards. A sack at the start of the fourth quarter pushed Sunyshore backward, but Watzon completed throws of seven and eleven to regain a first down. Later, facing third-and-ten, Alexander ran right for eleven. That conversion at 4:54 kept the possession alive and was an especially useful part of his 165-yard afternoon.

Duosion finished the twelve-play, 53-yard drive with a 44-yard field goal at 3:51. The lead was seven. Mahogany still had time, and the Frost began with an Exploud run for six. Porygon-Z added one on the ground before Anorith stopped Exploud for a one-yard loss on third-and-three. Watchog punted. The Starseekers received the ball with 2:31 remaining and did not give it back.

Alexander ran for four and then six. Watzon took the next third down up the middle for eleven yards. He followed with a nine-yard short-left completion to FLOAT SZN and a twelve-yard short-right pass to LaGatr. Two kneels ended the game. After the interceptions, Watzon had still supplied the run and completions required to make the last possession decisive.

Mahogany drops to 3–5 and hosts Hearthome next. Sunyshore visits a Lavender team that just surrendered a third-quarter lead at Blackthorn. Both clubs will have endings to discuss. Jones can point to a possession that began with 2:31 left, moved forty yards and consumed every remaining second. This time the Starseekers' final chance was enough.

art.alt: Scol Alexander, Scolipede No. 58, with a football in Sunyshore pink and black.

articles.title: Rustboro needed one yard. The defense made sure it got another try.
articles.dek: My Way, Son rushed for 151 yards, GET HIM! stopped a fourth-and-one, and two late Huntail recoveries helped the Stone finish a 14–0 shutout at Viridian.
articles.author: mara-voss

body.text: The most useful contrast in Rustboro's 14–0 win came on two fourth-and-one plays. Viridian handed the ball to Gabite with 4:13 left in the fourth quarter, trailing by seven. GET HIM! stopped the run left for no gain. On the next Rustboro possession, Philly took a fourth-and-one run up the middle for eleven yards. The Stone had denied the opponent the yard that mattered and then found considerably more than their own requirement.

That is a better explanation of the finish than simply admiring 223 rushing yards. Rustboro had moved the ball in its previous loss to Azalea, too. This time Tyler Scarboro's defense held the opponent scoreless, and the offense eventually completed the drive that put a tight game beyond one touchdown. My Way, Son rushed for 151 yards on sixteen carries and supplied the one-yard score with 1:55 left. The Stone improved to 4–4; Viridian fell to the same record.

The passing game provided only 58 yards. Rustboro converted one of five third downs. Two substantial drives ended on downs, and a fourth-quarter interception gave Viridian a genuine opportunity. There is plenty to correct. There is also a shutout and a closing possession that survived precisely the kind of awkward moment that had hurt the Stone one week earlier.
We kept getting useful carries, but the score stayed close. The defense gave us another possession after the interception. Finishing that one was the part we owed them.
body.speaker: My Way, Son

body.text: Seven points had to last a long time

The teams traded punts before Rustboro went 71 yards in ten plays. Porygon-Z finished the drive with a six-yard deep-right touchdown pass to Rufflet at 1:20 of the first quarter. Gorebyss added the extra point. The Stone would not score again until the final two minutes, which meant the defense spent most of the afternoon protecting a lead that one successful Viridian drive could erase.

The response after that touchdown was emphatic. Smoke Break sacked Mr. Rime for four yards on second-and-eight. Kricketune followed with a seven-yard sack on third-and-twelve. Viridian punted after losing nine yards on the possession. The Stone's pressure had made the first attempt to answer the touchdown considerably worse than a simple failure to gain a first down.

Rustboro's next drive traveled 52 yards and ended on downs. Viridian then held the ball for nineteen plays and 4:34, moving ninety yards before the half ended without a score. That possession is an unusually sharp reminder that movement and points are separate columns. The Titans had occupied almost the whole remaining quarter and still went to halftime down 7–0.

Mr. Rime completed nine of fifteen passes for 79 yards, with an interception and two sacks. Heatmor caught five passes for 33 yards. Gabite ran 21 times for ninety. Viridian gained eleven first downs and converted five of ten third downs, enough evidence of progress to prevent the afternoon from being described as a series of immediate failures. The Titans could get going. They could not finish a scoring possession.

Rustboro's defense allowed 173 total yards. That number reflects more than the two sacks, although those were important. The Stone also held the passing game to modest gains and took away the ball at two different stages of the closing stretch. Against an opponent capable of consuming a long possession, every stop protected the value of the early touchdown.
The lead survived two unfinished drives

After Viridian punted to start the second half, Rustboro moved 63 yards in nine plays and again turned the ball over on downs. The Stone had now built two long possessions without points after their opening touchdown. Scarboro did not have to borrow a concern from a different game. The same finishing problem had followed his offense into this one.

Milotic intercepted Mr. Rime's deep-left throw with 38 seconds left in the third quarter and returned it fifteen yards. Rustboro had another opportunity to extend the lead. My Way, Son opened the fourth quarter with an eleven-yard run up the middle, but Porygon-Z then threw an interception to Sigilyph, whose 32-yard return gave the Titans the ball with 5:30 left.

Viridian went immediately to Gabite: twelve yards left, seven up the middle, a one-yard loss right and three yards left. The sequence left fourth-and-one. GET HIM! stopped the next left run for no gain. The score remained 7–0, and the Stone received the ball with 4:12 remaining. A single failed yard had prevented a drive from becoming something much more dangerous.
We had to answer after giving them the ball. The stop gave us that chance. I want the offense to remember the relief of getting another possession, then remember what it took to keep it.
body.speaker: Tyler Scarboro

body.text: The defensive stand had several contributors. Smoke Break made the tackle for loss. Armaldo stopped the three-yard run that left the short fourth down. GET HIM! made the final tackle. Giving the entire possession to one name would miss how the preceding downs had created the chance to end it.
A recovery on each side of the touchdown

My Way, Son began Rustboro's next drive with gains of eight and fifteen. After an incompletion, he added nine up the middle. Another incomplete pass left fourth-and-one, and Philly gained eleven through the middle. After two earlier turnovers on downs in this game, the Stone had finally kept a crucial possession alive. This time the drive stayed alive.

Philly added three, and Porygon-Z found Shieldon short left for fifteen yards at the two-minute mark. The finish was almost interrupted. Philly fumbled on the next run, but SEARED BITE recovered for Rustboro. My Way, Son then ran right for the one-yard touchdown. Gorebyss' extra point made it 14–0 with 1:53 remaining.

On Viridian's next offensive snap, Gabite fumbled and another Rustboro Huntail recovered. These were two distinct plays and two different numbered Huntail: SEARED BITE, number 85, preserved the Stone's possession near the goal line; number 84 recovered the Titans' fumble after the kickoff. One prevented a damaging mistake. The other removed the opponent's last practical chance to answer.

My Way, Son followed with twelve yards up the middle, and Porygon-Z knelt twice. The quarterback's eight completions on seventeen attempts had produced little volume, but the touchdown to Rufflet and the late fifteen-yard throw to Shieldon mattered. SEARED BITE caught four passes for 29 yards. Philly finished with thirty rushing yards, Watchog with 23 and Gibby Timmy with thirteen. The offense's useful work extended beyond the leading runner, even if his 151 yards were the largest contribution.

Rustboro visits Celadon next; Viridian hosts Dewford. At 4–4, the Stone have recovered their balance and a current place in the conference's playoff positions. Scarboro still needs more complete possessions. He can begin the next meeting with the fourth-and-one stop at 4:13, the fourth-and-one conversion at 3:06 and the touchdown at 1:55. Three short distances, three very different consequences.

articles.title: Eterna makes you earn the last yard
articles.dek: Gardenia's defense keeps surviving the moments when a respectable gain ought to become a useful possession. Olivine spent an afternoon discovering the difference.
articles.author: mara-voss

body.text: I want to talk about the tackle after the completion. Yes, Eterna intercepted a pass. Yes, Klawf finally put Drampa on the ground. Those plays are easy to find. The Thorns' 19–0 win over Olivine was built just as surely out of receptions that went almost far enough. Gardenia's defense kept letting the Ironclads reach for the next down and then taking it away. That is a much better reason to take Eterna seriously than a tidy zero beside the opponent's name.

Start with 2:21 left in the second quarter. Olivine had third-and-five. Drampa threw short left to Grotle, who gained four before Tatsugiri made the tackle. The next snap came at the two-minute warning: fourth-and-one, Gabite running right, Komala stopping him for a loss of one. Two plays, two different defenders, one possession finished. The first tackle made the second possible. Give Tatsugiri his share of that stop before everyone runs toward the louder collision.

Eterna turned that possession into a touchdown. Slowking lost four on the first play, which was a fairly ungracious way to thank the defense. Then he found Marowak short left for fifteen, Ariados short left for six and Stantler short left for twelve and the score. Four snaps after the fourth-down stop, the lead was twelve. I don't need an elaborate tactical label for what Gardenia's team accomplished there. It earned a short route to points and completed the trip.
Tatsugiri kept the first one short. That gave us another chance to finish it. I was glad I could do my part on the next play.
body.speaker: Komala, Eterna

body.text: Komala's explanation is almost offensively modest for a linebacker who finished with six tackles. I'll supply the emphasis. Those are winning tackles. We spend an absurd amount of time admiring how a defense looks before the snap and far too little time asking whether it ends the play where it needs to. On those two downs, Eterna did. Jasmine's offense had a completion, a reasonable fourth-down distance and then a seat.
A completion is an unfinished sentence

The pattern had appeared long before that sequence. In the first quarter, Drampa found Delcatty short left on third-and-eleven. Six yards. Vanillish made the tackle, and Olivine punted. On the next possession, a third-and-six pass to Gabite gained one before Maushold ended it. Another punt. Those catches look harmless when you skim a passing line; in the context of the down, they are the entire argument. Eterna wasn't obliged to stop every completion. It had to stop the useful part.

Olivine converted two of ten third downs. It finished with 183 total yards, including 44 rushing yards from fifteen attempts. Those numbers describe an offense that occasionally moved and rarely sustained. Eterna's own attack made six of eleven third downs, which gave its defense something better than applause: time to wait between assignments. Both clubs punted five times. The difference was that the Thorns found three touchdowns among the other endings.

That distinction matters because this was hardly an afternoon of effortless Eterna offense. Slowking took three sacks. The running game produced twenty-four yards. Charjabug missed a field goal and two extra points. If Gardenia watches only the shutout and decides the entire operation is polished, I'll be furious on behalf of the people making those tackles. A defense this good deserves an offense that treats its work as an opportunity, not a standing invitation to try again.

There was plenty to build on. Slowking completed twenty-four of thirty-four passes for 249 yards, two touchdowns and no interceptions. Cramorant caught eight for 119. Ariados caught all six passes sent his way. Eterna can move the ball through the air without asking its defense to create every score. The task is to make those productive stretches appear often enough that a missed kick doesn't leave the whole afternoon resting on another third-down tackle.
I think we can give them more help. Cramorant kept getting us yards, and Ariados caught everything I put near him. There were chances for us to finish earlier.
body.speaker: Slowking, Eterna

body.text: The defensive work also survived actual setbacks. At 4:50 of the third quarter, Drampa hit Magmar deep right for twenty-three. Two more gains followed. Eterna then watched three consecutive passes fall incomplete, and Sunflora missed from forty-four yards. The missed kick belongs in the explanation; the defense doesn't get to claim it as a tackle. It does get credit for making Olivine attempt a field goal after a possession that had begun with a genuinely damaging completion.

Later in that quarter, Veluza caught passes for ten and twenty on consecutive snaps. Three plays after the second catch, Chesnaught stopped Gabite up the middle for no gain on third-and-eight. Punt. I love that sequence because it ruins the lazy version of the story. Olivine was capable of gaining yards. Eterna was capable of forcing a bad ending after allowing them. Those are different propositions, and the latter is the one that held up repeatedly.
The rush gets its turn

Klawf's sack came with 4:48 left in the fourth, on third-and-ten. Seven yards lost, another punt. Rampardos had six credited pressures in the game without a sack; Klawf had two pressures and the finish. That is why I won't use the sack column as a complete account of the pass rush. The record gives us several different kinds of contribution. It doesn't need us to invent a blitz package to make the work sound clever.

The Thorns are 4–3 with seventy-nine points scored and fifty-eight allowed. Mossdeep has allowed fifty-three in seven games; Saffron, forty-three in seven. Those are the company Eterna's defensive total keeps. Its three losses were 10–6, 10–6 and 7–3. That history makes me less interested in another stirring promise to keep opponents uncomfortable and much more interested in whether Slowking's side can turn its chances into something beyond single digits when the next tight game arrives.

Gardenia now takes this team to Cianwood. My demand is simple: preserve the tackling standard and give it a little more room to breathe. Cramorant supplied a useful example late against Olivine, catching twenty-one yards deep right on third-and-seven. Eterna eventually finished that possession with Deerling's four-yard touchdown. The defense had kept handing the ball back. This time the offense kept it long enough to put the game away.

And when Olivine got one final series, Komala was still there. Gabite caught a one-yard pass on second-and-two, then ran up the middle for nothing on third-and-one. Komala made both tackles. The Ironclads converted the fourth down afterward, but they never put points beside their name. Watch the catches. Then watch where they stop.

articles.title: Fortree finally gets a different question
articles.dek: After six losses and a succession of almosts, the Skyhawks beat Vermilion 34–10. The useful part is how much they did before the ending could become another argument.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: Rabsca has found a practical advantage to winning. The questions become shorter. There is less need to explain how close the team came, identify the one unfortunate moment or insist that everyone still believes in everyone else. After Fortree beat Vermilion 34–10, its quarterback could begin with three touchdown passes and allow the conversation to proceed from there. I suspect the Skyhawks would happily have accepted considerably less interesting questions for considerably fewer points.
I was starting to think you lot charged us by the explanation. Thirty-four points ought to get us a shorter interview. Put Basculegion in the headline; he'll be unbearable about it.
body.speaker: Rabsca, Fortree

body.text: Basculegion caught seven passes for sixty-six yards and two touchdowns, so the proposed headline would survive an editor. More to the point, Fortree won for the first time. Winona's team is 1–6. I would like to let that first digit exist for a moment without asking it to predict the next ten weeks. A first win is allowed to be a substantial event even when it doesn't cure everything that made the wait so long.

Last week, in this space, I wrote about Fortree losing 14–13 at Mahogany and never getting the ball again after Chinchou's late field goal. Four runs and two kneels finished that game. I argued that the Skyhawks needed specific work, particularly on protection and the late run defense, rather than another description of how nearly the score had gone their way. This week produced a pleasing complication: Fortree did so much earlier that the closing possessions could carry less weight.

The decisive passage, for me, began with 1:49 left before halftime. Vermilion had just made it 10–3. That is precisely the sort of score at which a winless club can spend the interval imagining every route toward disappointment. Fortree instead drove seventy-seven yards in eleven plays. Rabsca converted third-and-five with a short-right throw to Basculegion for fourteen, then later converted third-and-three with a short-left pass to Ariados for twelve. Both downs supplied an actual answer when the drive needed one.

With ten seconds left, Rabsca found Basculegion short right for an eight-yard touchdown. Chinchou made the extra point, and the Skyhawks led 17–3. It was a very useful time to be boringly accurate. The scoring pass was the last of a sequence that included a quarterback run, handoffs, completions to different receivers and two earlier incompletions. Fortree hadn't required every play to work. It had required the possession to survive the plays that didn't.
We all got a piece of that drive. Ariados kept it alive, Mothim moved us, Rabsca kept coming back to us. I got to be the one in the end zone. I'll take that job again.
body.speaker: Basculegion, Fortree

body.text: Basculegion's enthusiasm is easier to share when the next possession supports it. Fortree received the second-half kickoff, opened with two incompletions and then gained nine on a third-and-ten pass. There was the familiar invitation to let a promising afternoon become awkward. At 5:29 of the third quarter, Floatzel ran left on fourth-and-one and gained six. The drive remained Fortree's, which seems a small statement until you remember how much the Skyhawks had wanted another possession a week earlier.

Floatzel later caught a short-left pass for thirty yards on the same drive. Fearow added catches of four and twenty. Rabsca finished with a seven-yard scoring pass to Diglett, and the lead became 24–3 after the kick. The entire possession took ten plays and covered seventy-eight yards. Put those two touchdown drives beside one another: seventy-seven yards before halftime, seventy-eight after it. A team cannot produce that much sustained movement solely by waiting for somebody else to be generous.
A mistake no longer had to mean the afternoon

Vermilion did respond. Drakloak's sixty-three-yard catch helped set up a touchdown, and the Volts then forced a punt. Lt. Surge's team still had a route back into the game. Fortree answered that uncomfortable stretch when Volbeat fumbled a run left and Bewear recovered. Three plays later, Basculegion caught his second touchdown, this one an eleven-yard pass deep right. The Skyhawks had been interrupted; they had not been unravelled.

That is where the margin changes the experience of a game. At one point ahead, every mistake threatens to become the story. With an earlier body of good work behind you, a setback can remain a setback. Fortree had created room to survive a long opposing completion and an empty possession. I wouldn't mistake that room for a new personality trait. I would ask Winona to keep the two long touchdown drives somewhere prominent in the next week's discussion.

There was help from the other side of the ball throughout. Cyclizar intercepted a deep-right throw in the first quarter and returned it twenty-four yards, setting up Fortree's opening touchdown drive. Bewear recovered the later fumble and recorded a sack. The Volts gained 254 yards and scored ten points; Fortree finished with 362 and thirty-four. Rabsca's passing line was nineteen of thirty-two for 262 yards, three touchdowns and no interceptions. No lost fumble appears beside the Skyhawks, either.

The win also refuses a convenient rewrite of the opponent. Vermilion arrived 5–1. A twenty-four-point defeat doesn't make those five wins disappear, any more than Fortree's victory erases six losses. It does make the idea that the two records completely described these teams look rather thin. The Skyhawks had lost four of their previous five games by four points or fewer. They have now won one by twenty-four. Both sets of results belong to the same team.
We still have the same work. Get the yards we're asked for, hold the ball, do it again. Winning makes the week nicer. It doesn't shorten the next ten yards.
body.speaker: Floatzel, Fortree

body.text: There is also an injury report to keep the celebration in proportion. Ampharos, Pawmot and Mothim are each listed with two weeks remaining. Floatzel and Basculegion had minor entries, with no remaining absence recorded. Vermilion's Exploud, number eighty-seven, faces a much longer absence. None of that needs to be attached to an invented instant when the afternoon supposedly changed. It is the practical information both coaches carry away from a game whose score will be remembered more readily.

Next comes a trip to Fuchsia, another club with one win. I won't call that a formality after spending this much time objecting to what a record can conceal. Fortree has earned a week without the zero, and a chance to see whether its newly productive possessions travel. With forty-three seconds left against Vermilion, Rabsca knelt. With five seconds left, he did it again. For once, the final two kneels belonged to the Skyhawks.

articles.title: Hearthome, put the last first down on the poster
articles.dek: The Haunts survived a 14–13 game with 189 yards and an entire second half without points. Their best claim to the win arrived after the missed field goal.
articles.author: dorian-pike

body.text: Hearthome, I have selected your commemorative image. Resist the temptation to use a touchdown. Resist the temptation to print a tasteful photograph of the scoreboard and sell the word BELIEVE beneath it. Give me Haunter catching a ten-yard pass with 1:08 left in the fourth quarter. Give me the first down that finally allowed the Haunts to stop asking their defense for another favor. That is the picture. That is the play I would put on Fantina's wall.

The Haunts won 14–13 at Canalave. They gained 189 yards, made nine first downs and scored nothing after halftime. I offer those numbers with tremendous respect for everyone who would prefer I move immediately to the thrilling conclusion. We will get there. First, we are going to admit that a fourteen-point lead became a one-point lead while Hearthome's offense repeatedly returned to the sideline. A victory should not require its own accounting department to hide the bill.

And here's the uncomfortable truth: the Haunts finally earned the right to end this game when they stopped treating another possession as a prize somebody else needed to deliver. The defense had already supplied the opportunities. A missed field goal had supplied the last reprieve. At 1:13 remaining, Hearthome possessed the ball with a one-point lead and still had work to do. It completed that work. I am making a fuss because the completed part matters.
Three snaps, then quiet

Palafin ran right for two. Palafin ran up the middle for seven. On the recorded third-and-two, Frosmoth threw short middle to Haunter for ten yards. There it is. The final first down. The Haunts had asked their quarterback to finish an afternoon in which he threw for only 115 yards and had been intercepted once. He completed the throw that removed the need for another punt, another return and another desperate defensive series.
Throw it to me. I'll take responsibility for the catch. We had enough chances to finish that game, and I wanted this one to be ours.
body.speaker: Haunter, Hearthome

body.text: Good. More of that. Haunter finished with three receptions for forty-seven yards, including a twenty-three-yard catch on third-and-nine during the opening touchdown drive. The last catch was shorter and less decorative. Its value was enormous. Frosmoth knelt with twenty-seven seconds left. A team that had spent much of the second half trying to make fourteen points last finally held something more useful than hope: the ball, the lead and enough clock already gone.

Now give the people who kept that possibility alive their names. Komala made ten tackles and recovered a fumble. Araquanid made eight tackles. Solrock recorded a sack. Aromatisse made the fourth-down sack with 2:53 remaining, dropping Slowking for a loss of two. Hearthome's defense was asked to work while an opposing runner accumulated 131 yards. It was asked again after returns improved the opponent's position. The answer kept arriving at the moment the next gain threatened to become decisive.
We needed the ball back. Fourth down gave us one chance to do it.
body.speaker: Aromatisse, Hearthome

body.text: That sack did not end the suspense, because Hearthome's next series produced a run for no gain, a run for five and an incomplete pass on third-and-five. Punt. Sneasel returned it thirty-three yards. I will spare everyone the soothing claim that the Haunts were calmly controlling events. They had just used a magnificent defensive stop to purchase another defensive assignment. Fantina should enjoy the win and show that possession in full.

Komala then stopped a run right for a loss of two, made the tackle after an eight-yard completion, and watched Solrock hold the third-down run to two. The ensuing fifty-four-yard field goal went wide left with 1:16 remaining. The miss belongs to the kicker; Hearthome cannot claim to have steered it. The preceding stops belong to the Haunts. They helped leave a long attempt instead of a closer one, and the offense finally made use of the ball that followed.
Remember how the points arrived

There is a productive offense in this game if you know where to look. Hearthome's opening touchdown drive converted third-and-three on an eleven-yard Palafin run, another third-and-three on a six-yard pass to Castform, and third-and-nine on Haunter's twenty-three-yard reception. Palafin scored from one yard out. That is a possession with several answers. It is what makes the later inability to finish so irritating: the Haunts had already demonstrated the necessary vocabulary.

The second touchdown followed Gumshoos recovering a fumble on the opening snap of the second quarter. Frosmoth found Haunter for fourteen, then Wiglett for twenty-five. After an incompletion and a seven-yard Palafin run, Castform converted third-and-three with a five-yard catch. Palafin caught the seven-yard touchdown pass at 4:31. He supplied both Hearthome touchdowns, one rushing and one receiving. That is a considerably better use of a running back than asking him to explain why fourteen points ought to be sufficient.
We got the first two drives finished. After that we left too much for the defense. Those last two runs mattered because they gave us a down we could finish.
body.speaker: Palafin, Hearthome

body.text: Palafin had seventy-two rushing yards on eighteen carries and fourteen receiving yards on three catches. Those are useful contributions, not a license to declare the attack repaired. Hearthome went five-for-eleven on third down, punted five times and missed its only field-goal attempt. Frosmoth took no sacks, which removes one convenient excuse for every stalled possession. I want the quarterback and Fantina to demand more from the opportunities their protection did preserve.

I also want the Haunts to remember that they recovered two fumbles and turned only the first into points. The second, recovered by Komala at 3:46 of the second quarter, led to a two-yard run, two incompletions and a missed forty-nine-yard field goal. There was an earlier chance to make the afternoon less perilous. It existed. We are permitted to celebrate the result while being loud about the useful work left sitting on the table.

At 3–5, Hearthome has no reason to sneer at a one-point road win. It has every reason to extract something exact from it. Fantina can point to the early conversions, the two fumble recoveries and the late defensive stops. She can also demand that the final conversion become a habit: when the defense has handed you enough, finish the job yourself. The next trip is to Mahogany. Take the full game there, including the uncomfortable middle.

My verdict is that Hearthome earned this one in pieces and nearly returned several of them. The finish is worth keeping precisely because it was an action the Haunts performed. Palafin gained the yards. Frosmoth delivered the pass. Haunter caught it. Then came the kneel. Put that last first down on the poster, Fantina. Ten yards, and nobody else gets another turn.

articles.title: The Rook Board: Lapras leads, Klawf demands a second look
articles.dek: Calvin Rook ranks twelve offensive-line prospects, separates the two Eiscue files and refuses to let a workout become a promise.
articles.author: calvin-rook

body.text: The league just watched Snowpoint allow five sacks, Olivine score nothing and Saffron recover from two long drives that ended on downs. None of those results can be pinned entirely on five blockers. All of them are a useful reminder that drafting another exciting pass catcher does not remove the work required before the ball reaches that player. This week the Rook Board turns to offensive linemen.

Lapras from Agate State leads my twelve-player shortlist. Paniola State's Eiscue is close enough to demand serious comparison. Then comes the player I am choosing to argue about: Sunyshore's Klawf, whose workout earns third place despite a scouting band below Torkoal and Shuckle. That is my preference. It is not a secret exact grade disguised as an opinion.

The class offers sixty-four linemen with an available assessment. The ranges and combine numbers below are the information we have; they do not reveal a guaranteed ceiling, an exact rating or a development timetable. A fast cone can justify another look at movement. It cannot tell us that a prospect handled a particular pass-rush move in a game we have not watched.
Two Eiscue, two Shuckle, four separate decisions

Keep the schools attached to the names. Paniola State's Eiscue and Azalea's Eiscue are different prospects, as are the Shuckle from Mauville and Viridian State. Their ages, assessments and testing differ. If a scout starts discussing the name without the school, stop the conversation before the wrong file reaches the draft room.

The next circuit stop is the defensive line. For now, I would begin with Lapras, put the two leading Eiscue comparisons in order, and make someone explain why Klawf's workout should or should not change the football judgment. There are worse ways to spend a scouting meeting than arguing about who gets to keep the quarterback upright.

prospects.name: Lapras
prospects.analysis: Lapras is first because the available report begins higher than everyone else's, and the movement tests give me no compelling reason to argue with it. Agate State's prospect pairs a 4.95 forty with a 6.91 cone and a 33-inch vertical. That is an inviting starting point for a club trying to keep pressure away from its quarterback. I would investigate Lapras before building a draft plan around a receiver who needs extra time to get open.
prospects.concern: Seventeen bench reps do not settle how consistently the strength will show up against an IFL rusher. The 77–99 range is still a range.
prospects.projection: First OL on my board. Mossdeep should include Lapras in its succession scouting; that is a fit recommendation, not a prediction of availability.

prospects.name: Eiscue
prospects.analysis: Paniola State's Eiscue makes the strongest case for disturbing the top spot: the same 4.95 forty as Lapras, nineteen bench reps and an age of twenty-one. The 6.96 cone keeps the movement profile close. I prefer Lapras' higher lower bound today, but an additional report could change that conversation. A team with several line positions to refresh should be comparing these two before deciding it must solve the whole problem through an older acquisition.
prospects.concern: The 71–99 assessment overlaps Lapras substantially. Two extra bench reps do not prove superior blocking.
prospects.projection: Top-tier OL consideration. Keep the school attached to the name: another Eiscue appears lower on this board.

prospects.name: Klawf
prospects.analysis: Here is my deliberate departure from simply sorting the ranges. Sunyshore's Klawf runs 4.86, posts a 6.83 cone and completes 21 bench reps. Those are the best figures in those three tests among this selected group. I want to find out how much of that athletic promise becomes repeatable blocking. Fortree, after allowing two sacks even in its breakthrough win, is a club I would send to this workout with specific questions.
prospects.concern: The 65–93 scouting band sits below the top two. Athletic tests cannot certify anticipation, hand placement or a particular pass-protection assignment.
prospects.projection: My third lineman, on a bet about the profile rather than a claim that the uncertainty has disappeared.

prospects.name: Torkoal
prospects.analysis: Torkoal's 68–96 assessment earns a place near the front even though the 5.21 forty and 7.24 cone are less lively than Klawf's. Eighteen bench reps give the Cinnabar prospect a useful strength marker. I am willing to accept less straight-line speed for a lineman whose fuller report remains this promising. I am not willing to call the player a finished pass protector merely because the upper end of the range is attractive.
prospects.concern: At twenty-three, with the slower movement figures in this top group, Torkoal needs a clear football case beyond the headline band.
prospects.projection: Early OL shortlist; examine the assignment a team actually needs before moving Torkoal above the more mobile options.

prospects.name: Shuckle
prospects.analysis: Mauville's Shuckle is twenty-one with a 66–94 assessment. That is enough to make me keep the file open even when the testing—5.19 forty, sixteen bench reps and a 7.27 cone—does not demand a sprint to the podium. I like young line prospects who offer room for a team to learn more before committing its entire protection plan. Mauville's professional club should ask the same questions as everybody else, without letting the familiar university badge answer them.
prospects.concern: The broad range allows several different outcomes. Youth is not evidence of a particular development speed.
prospects.projection: Fifth on this board. A useful comparison with Torkoal for clubs choosing between age and the present assessment.

prospects.name: Audino
prospects.analysis: Audino's 35-inch vertical is the highest among these twelve, and the 5.00 forty is respectable company for it. Saffron Institute of Technology supplies a different sort of testing profile from Torkoal: fewer bench reps, more vertical pop and a quicker cone. The scouting range is 63–91. I want the next evaluation to connect those movement figures with actual blocking demands, particularly for an offense that repeatedly asks its line to sustain long passing possessions.
prospects.concern: Sixteen bench reps and a strong jump do not tell us how a defender gets handled at contact. The lower end of the band remains sixty-three.
prospects.projection: Middle of the leading OL group, with enough athletic interest to merit another look.

prospects.name: Tropius
prospects.analysis: North Orre's Tropius shares Audino's 63–91 assessment but reaches it through a slightly different testing sheet: 5.06 in the forty, seventeen bench reps, a 31-inch vertical and a 7.10 cone. At twenty-two, Tropius belongs in the same discussion rather than an entirely different tier. I would keep both reports together and ask which player better addresses the job the drafting club needs. The numbers here do not settle that distinction.
prospects.concern: There is no basis in the current information to name a specific line position or promise an immediate starter.
prospects.projection: Seventh, narrowly behind Audino. A reasonable target for another scouting visit when the first tier becomes expensive.

prospects.name: Eiscue
prospects.analysis: This is the Azalea University Eiscue, age twenty-three, not Paniola State's twenty-one-year-old. The 4.92 forty is slightly quicker, but the 60–88 assessment starts materially lower. Seventeen bench reps and a 33-inch vertical keep the testing interesting. A name repeated on a draft list is an invitation to read carelessly; do not let the stronger Eiscue's reputation become a free endorsement of this one.
prospects.concern: The 7.09 cone trails the other Eiscue's 6.96, and neither comparison overrides the broader scouting gap.
prospects.projection: Second group of OL prospects. Potentially useful value if a club has done the identity-specific homework.

prospects.name: Spiritomb
prospects.analysis: Spiritomb moves above Lickitung on my list because eighteen bench reps and a 7.08 cone make the Blackthorn State prospect's testing more persuasive to me. The 59–87 band is slightly lower, so this is a judgment call rather than an arithmetic victory. The 5.09 forty is ordinary within this group. I would ask a protection-needy club such as Snowpoint to compare the whole sheet before deciding a one-point difference in the band has settled the order.
prospects.concern: The report still covers a large span, and these tests do not establish that Spiritomb would prevent any particular sack we watched this week.
prospects.projection: Ninth. A comparison prospect for teams that want strength and movement evidence without paying for the top headline.

prospects.name: Stunfisk
prospects.analysis: Castelia's Stunfisk is twenty-one, runs 5.02 and posts a 7.00 cone. The 58–86 assessment is less commanding than the early names, but the movement figures keep this player above a few higher-band alternatives on my personal board. I would rather explain that preference openly than hide it behind a supposedly exact ranking. Several clubs need line options; not every one of them will be drafting early enough to choose Lapras.
prospects.concern: Fifteen bench reps leave strength questions worth investigating. A younger age does not resolve them.
prospects.projection: Tenth, with interest for teams comparing the second group on a narrower budget of premium selections.

prospects.name: Lickitung
prospects.analysis: Lickitung brings a 60–88 assessment and an age of twenty-one. Those are the reasons the Cortondo prospect remains in this group despite twelve bench reps, a 27-inch vertical and a 7.34 cone. I can imagine a later report making the player more appealing; I cannot treat that imagined report as something already received. Put Lickitung beside Spiritomb and ask why the assessment and testing suggest different orders.
prospects.concern: The testing trails several neighboring candidates. Do not convert the top of the scouting band into a certainty merely to make the fit attractive.
prospects.projection: Eleventh. Further scouting is the strongest recommendation I can make before attaching an aggressive draft price.

prospects.name: Shuckle
prospects.analysis: Viridian State's Shuckle closes the board with a 57–85 assessment, fifteen bench reps and a 7.25 cone. The 5.24 forty will not be the workout's main selling point. At twenty-three, this Shuckle also differs meaningfully from Mauville's younger prospect. I am including the player to show where the leading shortlist currently ends, not to pretend the sixty-four visible OL candidates can be reduced to twelve certain outcomes.
prospects.concern: The lower assessment and modest testing both require a persuasive follow-up before a club commits a starting job.
prospects.projection: Twelfth on this week's shortlist. Keep reviewing the rest of the class; a place here is an editorial preference, not a completed evaluation.

art.alt: Football, gloves and blocking equipment for the offensive-line draft board.

articles.title: The Pecking Order: what keeps you up at night?
articles.dek: Mossdeep rests, Mt. Silver keeps winning, and several contenders discover that the injury report does not care about their place in the table.
articles.author: rowan-vale

body.text: I gave Mossdeep the week off and still found reasons to worry about everybody else. Saffron scored 44 unanswered points and lost Verrick Brooks for four weeks. Sunyshore ran for 221 yards and lost Myles Gabite for five. Mt. Silver threw two interceptions and won by 25 anyway, which is chiefly a concern for the rest of the league.

This week's question is what keeps each club awake. Eterna climbs because its defense has earned more than polite appreciation. Fortree climbs because winning 34–10 is a more persuasive rebuttal than telling me it was always better than 0–6. Vermilion falls because someone has to account for being on the other side of that argument. The rankings are my judgment about the teams now; the standings remain entirely entitled to disagree.
Last week I had Eterna fourteenth and Olivine twelfth. The Thorns won 19–0. Consider the order corrected. I reserve the right to make a fresh mistake before the end of this page.

articles.theme: What keeps you up at night?

rankings.text: Michael Dorrill's 7–0 team took the week off. It still owns a 307–53 scoring advantage and my top spot. Cerulean gets the first chance to discover whether the bye made the Eclipse rusty. My working assumption is that rust will find somewhere safer to live.

Eight wins, no losses, and a 34–9 result with two interceptions thrown. Mt. Silver scored on a kickoff return and a pick-six. Connor McLarren has assembled a team that can survive a quarterback's bad decision by changing the department responsible for the next touchdown.

The Psi Corps scored 44 unanswered points and lost Verrick Brooks for four weeks. Ninetales is out four as well. I can adore Archam Manning's 86-yard return and still wonder who replaces thirteen sacks. My favorite team has provided both the fireworks and the bill.

Hatterene completed 27 of 29 for 307 yards. The Dragons erased an eleven-point deficit, then scored twice in twenty-four seconds of fourth-quarter clock. I ranked them fourth last week. Apparently they decided two incompletions were enough resistance from the outside world.

A 17–6 win takes the Blaze to 6–2 with eighty points allowed. Mauville's two interceptions helped, but the defense also recorded three sacks. Petalburg arrives next with a considerably better record than the Dynamos. Blaine gets a useful test of how portable that defensive control really is.

Scol Alexander ran for 165 yards, and Sunyshore finally kept the last possession. Fine work. Myles Gabite is now out five weeks, and the passing game still threw two interceptions against Mahogany. Karson Jones has a 6–2 team and several reasons to keep the meeting going.

The 5–2 Pride rested while most of the league demonstrated fresh ways to make winning difficult. Cinnabar awaits. Norman should bring the late-touchdown version of his offense and ask the defense for another possession this time. The bye did not change a very respectable seventh place.

Up six spots after a 19–0 shutout, and yes, I noticed the offense finally helped. Eterna has allowed 58 points in seven games. Its three losses came with six, six and three points scored. Gardenia's defense deserves a teammate that occasionally buys dinner.

The Tide followed their 12–6 win over Sunyshore with a bye. Now Mossdeep visits. Four successful field goals made last week's win; I suspect Misty would appreciate a touchdown or two for this appointment. A 4–3 record keeps Cerulean relevant, not comfortable.

Five places upward for a 14–0 road shutout. My Way, Son ran for 151 yards, GET HIM! stopped Viridian on fourth-and-one, and Philly converted Rustboro's own short fourth down. Tyler Scarboro can put those two clips beside last week's unfinished drives and let the contrast do the talking.

A 14–13 loss despite 168 rushing yards is an excellent way to ruin a good running-back afternoon. Two lost fumbles and a late missed field goal supplied the explanation. The Bulwark are 5–3 with 103 points scored and 103 allowed. Even the totals refuse to choose a side.

The Breakers beat Pewter 14–7 despite two interceptions. At 4–4, they have returned to the middle of the argument. The trip to Viridian offers a chance to stay there. I like the recovery; I would like the offense to stop requiring forgiveness quite so often.

Down five after losing 34–10 to previously winless Fortree. Exploud, number 87, is out twelve weeks, and a 5–2 record now sits beside a plus-one point differential. Lt. Surge has five wins he can keep and a fresh result he cannot explain with those five wins.

A 17–0 win with 350 yards to Cianwood's 106 moves the Swarm up two. They waited until the second quarter to score, then stopped making the game mysterious. Drampa threw for 249 yards. Bugsy has a 4–4 club and, for once, a pleasant set of comparisons.

The Titans gained ninety yards on a possession that ended with the first-half clock, then were stopped on fourth-and-one in the fourth. Zero points followed. At 4–4, Viridian has become a warning against treating distance traveled as a scoring system. Dewford arrives next.

Lavender moves up three because its 27–17 loss at Blackthorn was a real competitive response to the Mossdeep collapse. The Wails still led 17–6 and lost. Travis Scarboro gets credit for the opening drives and a very specific question about the closing ones. Sunyshore will ask it again.

The Frost forced three Sunyshore turnovers and still lost 17–10. Twenty carries produced 22 yards. Three-and-five with a positive point differential is a fascinating conversation starter; a functioning rushing series would be more useful. Hearthome visits after surviving its own one-point drama.

Iron Jugulis attempted 51 passes in a 13–9 victory. Gurdurr caught thirteen for 113 yards. The Falcons are 3–4, and apparently their preferred answer to a close game is to keep the receiver very busy. Pastoria is next; a little more scoring would make the volume easier to admire.

Veilstone punted eight times, converted one of eleven third downs and won 17–10. Three interceptions of Oreburgh supplied a ladder out of the hole. The Fists occupy the last current conference playoff position at 4–4. Blackthorn is unlikely to hand them the same ladder.

Up seven for a 14–13 road win. The defense kept providing chances until the offense finally converted the first down that ended it. Fantina should frame Haunter's ten-yard catch and keep the empty second-half possessions in a less decorative folder. Three-and-five is better than the alternative.

A 19–0 loss and two successful third downs in ten attempts move the Ironclads down nine. Several catches ended just short of being useful. Eterna did the tackling; Olivine supplied the recurring disappointment. A home game with Oreburgh offers a chance to produce something beyond an explanation.

Up nine after the Skyhawks beat a 5–1 opponent by 24. Rabsca threw three touchdowns, and Fortree built scoring drives of 77 and 78 yards around halftime. One-and-six is still one-and-six. It now includes proof that Winona's offense can do considerably more than lose attractively.

Dragapult threw two interceptions in a 17–6 loss, while Cinnabar swatted nine passes. Three-and-five is survivable; continuing to finish possessions without touchdowns is less appealing. The Dynamos visit Pewter, where the scoring expectations have been known to arrive in a very small envelope.

Three field goals were all the Blizzard managed against Mt. Silver. The Reds scored five touchdowns across offense, defense and returns. Snowpoint's 2–6 record does not erase some useful rushing work, but it does make the bye an excellent time to discuss five sacks allowed.

The Bloom closed a 17–13 win with runs that denied Fuchsia another turn. Delibird caught five passes for 104 yards and a touchdown. Celadon rises five places, which is what happens when the bottom of my table finally supplies something better than an apology.

A 14–7 defeat leaves the Rockers with 64 points in eight games. Two interceptions should have bought more than another discussion of a one-score loss. Pewter hosts Mauville next. I have asked the scoreboard operator to remain awake on the grounds that anything is possible.

The Miners outgained Veilstone 188–181 and still lost 17–10 because Cryogonal threw three picks. Thievul's last interception ended the late attempt to tie. Oreburgh is 2–6, and an offense this short on surplus yards cannot keep returning its possessions as gifts.

rankings.themeLabel: The opening kickoff of the half
rankings.text: Leading Saffron 9–7 at halftime was an achievement. Allowing 37 second-half points was the rest of the afternoon. The Waves are 2–5 and head to Violet. They should take Kilowattrel's 53-yard touchdown with them and leave the second-half special-teams experience in the review room.

Seven punts, four completions and a 17–0 defeat. Cianwood's runners gained 73 yards, but the passing game produced 33. Eterna arrives next with a defense that just shut out Olivine. Chuck needs a much better answer than hoping the visitor has become bored with tackling.

The Surge lost 13–9 at Violet, and Heatmor is out six weeks. At 3–4 they still have more wins than several clubs above them here. My rankings are allowed to notice the minus-44 point differential and the trip to Saffron. Those are less reassuring companions.

Celadon converted a late third-and-three by running for eight and never returned the ball. Fuchsia fell to 1–7 and lost Kleavor for ten weeks. The Shadows host Fortree next. Somebody has to leave that meeting with a second win unless both decide to make my job worse.

The Inferno rested at 2–5 with 203 points allowed. Fortree's first win supplies an awkward divisional comparison: the Skyhawks just scored 34 against the same Vermilion club Lavaridge visits next. A week off is useful only if the next week looks different.
